title: Who Survived the Donner Party
text:
In the spring of 1846, a group of emigrant families left Illinois and the Midwest for California. On bad advice they took an untested shortcut, the Hastings Cutoff, which cost them weeks. By late October they were trapped by early snow in the Sierra Nevada, near what is now Donner Lake. Of the eighty-seven people in the group, nearly half died over the winter from cold, starvation and exhaustion, and some survivors resorted to eating the dead.

Nearly a century and a half later, the anthropologist Donald Grayson examined who lived and who died. His study, published in 1990, found a strong pattern. Age and sex mattered: young children and the elderly died at high rates, and women survived better than men. But one of the clearest factors was family. People traveling with large family groups were much more likely to survive than those traveling alone. Most of the young single men, the teamsters and hired hands who had joined the group without relatives, died.

Grayson suggested a reason. Family members shared food, warmth and care with one another when there was not enough for everyone. Someone alone in the snow had no one whose survival was bound up with his own. The Reed family, for example, lost no members, while many of the solitary men were among the first to die.
lesson: In a crisis, the people bound to us matter more than strength. Building and keeping close ties is a form of survival, not only of comfort.
people: Donner Party members; Donald K. Grayson
source: Donald K. Grayson (1990). Donner Party deaths: A demographic assessment. Journal of Anthropological Research, 46(3), 223 to 242
caveat: The exact numbers vary slightly between accounts because membership of the party is counted in different ways.
